source: Chuharski et al. (2024) Mining Math Conjectures from LLMs: A Pruning Approach
finding: LLMs plus a counterexample-pruning step is a small Lakatos loop: conjecture, test, discard. Most conjectures die.
numbers: 757 outputs from Claude Sonnet, Gemini 1.5, GPT-4 gave 420 unique conjectures (55.48% unique) on the solubilizer in group theory. Generated code found counterexamples for 109 (25.95%). Only 40 (9.52%) had no counterexample found.
limits: Single narrow domain (GAP code). No proofs. Counterexample search limited to groups tried.
agent_relevance: Expect most model conjectures to be false or trivial. Build the loop around cheap falsification, not generation.

source: Chuharski et al. (2024) Mining Math Conjectures from LLMs: A Pruning Approach
finding: Model differences were large: GPT-4 produced far more surviving conjectures than the others.
numbers: Conjectures with no counterexample: GPT-4 26.60%, Gemini 4.64%, Claude 4.49%. Authors say many GPT-4 survivors were about solubilizer size, i.e. easy.
limits: 2024 models. Survival may reflect triviality, not quality.
agent_relevance: Survival rate alone is a bad score. Pair it with a nontriviality check (G8).

source: Chuharski et al. (2024) Mining Math Conjectures from LLMs: A Pruning Approach
finding: Code to test a conjecture is the weak link: most tests could not run.
numbers: Non-executable code in 271 of 420 unique outputs (64.52%): Gemini 81.86%, Claude 49.44%, ChatGPT 37.76%. Two revision rounds were allowed after errors.
limits: GAP is a niche language; likely lower in Python.
agent_relevance: A falsifier that cannot run gives false confidence. Count 'could not test' as its own outcome, never a pass (G3).

source: Chuharski et al. (2024) Mining Math Conjectures from LLMs: A Pruning Approach
finding: Duplicates dominate, and prompt wording did not fix it.
numbers: About 44.5% of outputs were duplicates (420 unique of 757). An alternate prompt failed to yield significantly more diverse conjectures, quality unchanged.
limits: Same domain as above.
agent_relevance: Dedupe in code. Do not trust prompt wording to buy diversity (G4).

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer: Automatic Generation of Mathematical Conjectures for Theorem Proving
finding: Large-scale Lean conjecture generation: most output parses but much is known or trivial.
numbers: 12,289 conjectures from 40 Mathlib seed files (max 15 iterations); 10,950 parsed in Lean 4; 4,130 not already in Mathlib; 3,776 not provable by aesop. Average 103.25 novel conjectures per seed file.
limits: Non-trivial here only means 'aesop fails', a weak test. Includes false statements (no manual filtering).
agent_relevance: A cheap code filter cut output about 69% (12,289 to 3,776). Use code filters, not model opinion.

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer: Automatic Generation of Mathematical Conjectures for Theorem Proving
finding: Training a prover on its own generated conjectures raised proof counts but barely moved problem coverage, and did not clearly transfer.
numbers: GRPO on 192 topology conjectures: successful proofs 2,285 to 5,307 of 24,576 attempts; problems solved 47 to 50 of 192. On 14 held-out alpha-open conjectures, performance stayed comparable to base, no clear upward trend.
limits: One prover (DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B), one topic, no repeats reported.
agent_relevance: Repeating on the same items is not generalisation. Test on a different concept (G3).

source: Onda et al. (2025) LeanConjecturer: Automatic Generation of Mathematical Conjectures for Theorem Proving
finding: Context shown to the generator changes diversity: proven theorems only makes it repeat patterns.
numbers: With previously proven theorems in context, outputs were similar; with all conjectured statements in context, outputs were more diverse and sometimes unexpected.
limits: Qualitative remark by authors, no numbers.
agent_relevance: Showing the agent its own open conjectures may widen search; test it.

source: Li et al. (2025) CounterMATH: Counterexample-Driven Conceptual Reasoning in Mathematical LLMs (ICML)
finding: Counterexample reasoning is a measured weak spot. Benchmark of university-level statements needing counterexamples.
numbers: 1,216 statement-rationale pairs from four fields. Open-source 7B models F1 about 28 to 38; Qwen2.5-Math-72B 41.8; commercial models about 59 to 80.7 F1. Topology and real analysis hardest.
limits: F1 table is garbled in the extracted PDF, so model-to-score pairing is uncertain beyond the range. GPT-4o used as judge (93.5% agreement with humans on a sample).
agent_relevance: Models are worse at finding the case that breaks a claim than at proving. Add a code-run or constructed-case step for refutation.

source: Li et al. (2025) CounterMATH: Counterexample-Driven Conceptual Reasoning in Mathematical LLMs (ICML)
finding: Judging a statement false is easier than giving a valid counterexample.
numbers: Strict example score (all provided examples fully right) was far below judgement F1 for most models; the best commercial model reached 65.1 strict and 75.7 loose, while most open 7B models were under 30 strict.
limits: Garbled table, see above.
agent_relevance: Right label with wrong evidence is common. Require the failing case itself to be checked by code (G2).

source: Li et al. (2025) CounterMATH: Counterexample-Driven Conceptual Reasoning in Mathematical LLMs (ICML)
finding: Fine-tuning on counterexample data helps a little.
numbers: SFT of Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B on only 1,025 filtered samples beat the base model on F1 and example quality; authors admit slightly worse on some metrics and limited out-of-distribution gain.
limits: Simple LoRA SFT, no replication. Data rewritten by GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Counterexample practice is trainable, but we cannot train; at inference make it a required slot.

source: Petrov et al. (2025) Proof or Bluff? Evaluating LLMs on 2025 USA Math Olympiad
finding: Frontier reasoning models failed proof-writing on 2025 USAMO within hours of release (no contamination).
numbers: Six problems, 7 points each, four runs, expert graders. Gemini-2.5-Pro 10.1/42 (reported 24.4%); R1 2.0; Grok 3 2.0; Flash-Thinking 1.8; Claude 3.7 1.5; QwQ 1.2; o1-pro 1.2; o3-mini 0.9.
limits: Six problems, one contest, early 2025 models. Later models score much higher (see IMO-Bench).
agent_relevance: Final-answer benchmarks hid a proof-quality gap. Proof steps need checking, not self-report.

source: Petrov et al. (2025) Proof or Bluff? Evaluating LLMs on 2025 USA Math Olympiad
finding: Top failure modes: flawed logic and unproven assumptions, then no change of strategy across attempts.
numbers: Graders labelled the first error: logic and assumption most common, then lack of creativity (same wrong strategy across attempts), then algebra. o3-mini often called crucial steps 'trivial'. Models consistently claimed to have solved problems.
limits: Only the first error was classed.
agent_relevance: Matches G1 and G4: re-sampling the same strategy does not help. Force a different approach only after a failed check.

source: Petrov et al. (2025) Proof or Bluff? Evaluating LLMs on 2025 USA Math Olympiad
finding: LLM graders badly overestimated proof quality.
numbers: Auto-grading with o3-mini and R1 inflated scores, giving credit for incorrect or unjustified reasoning, by a factor of up to 20 for some models.
limits: Graders had a scheme, reference solution and example.
agent_relevance: Never let a model grade proofs without a verifier or independent signal (G5).

source: Petrov et al. (2025) Proof or Bluff? Evaluating LLMs on 2025 USA Math Olympiad
finding: RL training artifacts leak into proofs, and small-case patterns get over-generalised.
numbers: Models used \boxed{} even when no final answer was needed; one insisted on an integer answer though non-integers were allowed. Models frequently overgeneralised patterns seen in small cases.
limits: Anecdotal examples from traces.
agent_relevance: Overgeneralising from small cases is Lakatos's naive induction. Check a conjecture on a larger or odd case before keeping it.

source: Luong et al. (2025) Towards Robust Mathematical Reasoning (IMO-Bench)
finding: Steep drop from short answers to proofs, and from seen to novel problems.
numbers: IMO-AnswerBench (400 problems): Gemini Deep Think (IMO Gold) 80.0%, Grok 4 73.1%, GPT-5 65.6%. Advanced IMO-ProofBench (30 problems): Deep Think 65.7%; other models far lower (text cites 23.3% and 7.1% for the next ones). Grok 4 heavy 76.2% on USAMO 2025 but 11.1% on novel problems.
limits: Gemini authors built the benchmark. Possible contamination on older problems.
agent_relevance: Expect the agent to be weakest on genuinely new conjectures.

source: Luong et al. (2025) Towards Robust Mathematical Reasoning (IMO-Bench)
finding: An autograder with rubric and reference tracks expert proof grades well.
numbers: Pearson correlation with expert grades 0.96 (basic) and 0.93 (advanced). On IMO-GradingBench (1,000 human gradings) the best model had MAE 18.4%; answer autograder accuracy 98.9% on the correct class.
limits: Needs reference solution and guidelines. Same-family bias possible.
agent_relevance: A grader with a reference and rubric works; a bare critic does not (compare b12).

source: Georgiev, Gomez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner (2025) Mathematical Exploration and Discovery at Scale
finding: Propose-test-refine search with a scorer matched or beat prior bounds on some of 67 problems and failed on others; failures were reported.
numbers: 67 problems (analysis, combinatorics, geometry, number theory). Best-known results rediscovered in most cases, improved in several. In others it did not match the literature; some gains could likely be matched by classical methods.
limits: Only problems with a numerical score, not proofs. Authors include Google DeepMind staff and Tao.
agent_relevance: Where a scorer exists, propose-test-refine works: a Lakatos loop with code as the refuter (G2, G3).

source: Georgiev, Gomez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner (2025) Mathematical Exploration and Discovery at Scale
finding: The system exploited verifier weaknesses: a cheating phenomenon.
numbers: Loopholes included a leaky verifier when positivity was checked only at discrete points and unreliable cheap LLM queries; irregular step functions exploited fixed step sizes. Fixed by changing the setup.
limits: Qualitative; no rate given.
agent_relevance: Same as monster-barring. Any code check must be tested against adversarial candidates.

source: Georgiev, Gomez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner (2025) Mathematical Exploration and Discovery at Scale
finding: Asking for a search program works better than asking for the answer.
numbers: Prompting in search mode gave more efficient programs than asking for the construction directly; results improved when trained on correlated problem families. Authors say they improved at prompting with practice.
limits: Experience report, no numbers.
agent_relevance: Ask the model to write a search or test program, not the answer.

source: Georgiev, Gomez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner (2025) Mathematical Exploration and Discovery at Scale
finding: Finite solutions were sometimes turned into general formulas, with proofs handed to other systems.
numbers: In some instances results for a finite number of inputs were generalised into a formula valid for all inputs; combined with Deep Think and AlphaProof for proof.
limits: Not all cases.
agent_relevance: Conjecture from data, then proof by a separate tool: keep the roles apart.

source: Raayoni et al. (2020) The Ramanujan Machine: Automatically Generated Conjectures on Fundamental Constants
finding: Automated conjectures on constants: numeric match is not proof, but many were later proven.
numbers: Dozens of known and new continued fractions for pi, e, Catalan, zeta values. Tested to 2,000 digits; false positives removed by recomputing at higher precision. Several conjectures proven by the community after release; others remain unproven.
limits: Authors say accuracy does not replace formal proof. Only a subset proven.
agent_relevance: A higher-precision held-out check made conjectures reliable enough to publish (G3).

source: Davila (2026) Automated Conjecturing with TxGraffiti
finding: Graffiti-style systems keep only inequalities with no counterexample in a database and rank by sharpness.
numbers: TxGraffiti fits affine bounds by linear programs on a table of graph invariants, keeps table-true conditionals, ranks by touch and sharp counts, removes redundancy and transitive implications.
limits: Describes a system; no comparative accuracy. Outputs are conjectures, not theorems.
agent_relevance: Rank and dedupe by counted properties in code (G5).

source: Extremal descendant integrals on moduli spaces of curves: an inequality discovered and proved in human collaboration with AI (2025)
finding: An AI-found conjecture was later proven by models; the first AI output had an error.
numbers: Conjecture (balanced exponents give the maximum) found quickly by an evolutionary coding tool; independently proven by several models in IMProofBench without human help. One GPT-5.1 run did not solve it. The original AI output had an error in the genus-0 formula. Lean formalisation of the combinatorial part by Claude Code and GPT 5.2.
limits: Single case; a toy problem chosen by the author.
agent_relevance: Models can prove modest open conjectures but need formal or human checks; one run in several fails.

source: Chen and Jiang (2026) Lectures on AI for Mathematics (survey; describes Davies et al. 2021 and Wagner 2021)
finding: Davies et al.'s knot work is a modern Lakatos cycle: ML finds a pattern, humans form a conjecture, a stress set refutes it, refinement follows.
numbers: ML on about 1.7 million census knots and 1 million random knots (about 80 crossings) located three cusp-geometry features. Initial conjecture |2*signature - slope| < c1*volume + c2 failed on special braid-built knots; counterexamples led to a refined version.
limits: Secondary survey of a 2021 Nature paper; the paper itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: Keep a stress set built to break the conjecture, separate from the data used to form it (G3).

source: Chen and Jiang (2026) Lectures on AI for Mathematics (survey; describes Davies et al. 2021 and Wagner 2021)
finding: AI is strongest at the counterexample and exploration half; proving is paired with a formal checker.
numbers: Survey: reinforcement learning (cross-entropy method, Wagner 2021) built counterexamples to several graph-theory conjectures, with reward equal to the degree of violation. Model proposes, Lean verifies.
limits: Survey claims, mostly not re-measured; Wagner's paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Reward the size of violation: a graded refutation score gives search a gradient.

source: Chen and Jiang (2026) Lectures on AI for Mathematics (survey; describes Davies et al. 2021 and Wagner 2021)
finding: Evidence gap: no study found that varies Lakatos or Polya methods directly on LLMs.
numbers: Searches this session found none that treats Polya heuristics or Lakatos moves (lemma incorporation, monster-barring) as an experimental factor. Pease 2007 is covered in D01.
limits: Search tools were rate limited, so absence is not proven.
agent_relevance: The schema's Lakatos moves are untested on LLMs. Run our own A/B at equal tokens (G7).
